subject: math
title: Compare Fractions
seo_title: Grade 4 Comparing Fractions Worksheets: Common Denominators, Common Numerators and Benchmark 1/2
standard_text: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators, e.g., by creating common denominators or numerators, or by comparing to a benchmark fraction such as 1/2. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 comparing fractions worksheets: compare fractions with models, common denominators, common numerators and the benchmark 1/2, order fractions, and solve word problems. 100 practice questions with explanations and a printable answer key.
key_big: To compare fractions, make the pieces the same size, make the number of pieces the same, or compare each one to 1/2.
key_sub: 2/3 and 3/4 become 8/12 and 9/12, so 2/3 < 3/4. Fractions can only be compared when they are parts of the same whole.
body_html:
The idea

A fraction’s size depends on both numbers: how many pieces, and how big each piece is. To compare two fractions, make one of these the same, or compare each fraction to an easy fraction like 12.

Write the result with a symbol: > (greater than), < (less than) or = (equal). The open side of the symbol faces the bigger fraction.

Strategy 1: Make a common denominator

Cut the pieces so both fractions have the same size pieces. Then compare the top numbers. Multiply the top and bottom by the same number.

Example

Compare 56 and 34.

Use twelfths: 56 = 1012 and 34 = 912. 10 > 9.

Answer: 56 > 34

Strategy 2: Make a common numerator

If the top numbers are the same, you have the same number of pieces. Then the fraction with the smaller bottom number has bigger pieces, so it is greater.

Example

Compare 34 and 610.

34 = 68. Eighths are bigger than tenths, so 68 > 610.

Answer: 34 > 610

Strategy 3: Compare to 12 or 1

Is the top number more or less than half of the bottom number? If one fraction is less than 12 and the other is more, you are done.

WhenTryExample
One bottom number is a multiple of the otherCommon denominator35 and 710: 610 < 710
The top numbers are easy to matchCommon numerator12 and 38: 36 > 38
One is below 12, one is aboveBenchmark 1225 < 712
One is more than 1, one is lessBenchmark 154 > 78

Use the same whole

Fractions can only be compared when they are parts of the same size whole. 13 of a long bar can be longer than 12 of a short bar, but 13 is still less than 12.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Thinking 18 > 15 because 8 > 5A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces
Comparing only the top numbers: 38 > 23Check the piece size too: 38 is less than 12
Adding the same number to the top and bottom: 23 = 1112Multiply the top and bottom by the same number: 23 = 812
Saying 23 = 34 because each is 1 piece from a wholeThe missing pieces are different sizes: 13 > 14
Comparing parts of different-size wholesMake sure both fractions are of the same whole

faq.q: How do you compare fractions with different denominators?
faq.a: Rewrite them with a common denominator, then compare the numerators. For 2/3 and 3/4, use twelfths: 8/12 is less than 9/12, so 2/3 < 3/4.
A benchmark is an easy fraction you compare to, usually 1/2 or 1. If 3/8 is less than 1/2 and 4/6 is more than 1/2, then 3/8 < 4/6.

faq.q: Why must fractions refer to the same whole?
faq.a: A fraction is part of a whole, so its size depends on the whole. Half of a small pizza can be less than a third of a large pizza.

faq.q: How do you tell if a fraction is more than 1/2?
faq.a: Compare the top number with half of the bottom number. In 5/8, half of 8 is 4 and 5 is more than 4, so 5/8 is more than 1/2.
